title: The Psalm That Described the Crucifixion Before It Happened
paragraphs: The Psalm That Described the Crucifixion Before It Happened
Some people stumble over the cross because they see it as a tragedy.
Others reject it because they see it as weakness.
But there is another reason many never truly look at the crucifixion.
Because if the cross was written before it happened, then the cross was never an accident.
And if the cross was never an accident, then neither is your story.
Long before Roman soldiers drove nails into human flesh.
Long before a crown of thorns pressed into the brow of Jesus.
Long before the hill called Golgotha became the center point of human history.
A shepherd sat beneath Middle Eastern skies and wrote words he could not possibly understand.
Words that would echo across a thousand years.
Words that would eventually describe the death of the Messiah with astonishing precision.
Those words became Psalm 22.
And once you see it, you may never read the crucifixion account the same way again.
The story begins not with a king.
Not with a cross.
Not even with Jesus.
It begins with a cry.
"My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?"
In Hebrew:
"אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי"
Eli, Eli, lama azavtani.
(Psalm 22:1)
More than a thousand years later, hanging from the cross, Jesus cried:
"Ἠλί Ἠλί, λιμὰ σαβαχθανί"
Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani.
(Matthew 27:46)
Matthew preserves the Aramaic expression spoken by Jesus.
The meaning is the same:
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
Many standing near the cross thought Jesus was simply crying out in agony.
But Jewish listeners would have recognized something profound.
When rabbis referenced the opening line of a psalm, they often intended the entire psalm to be recalled.
Jesus was not merely expressing suffering.
He was directing attention to Psalm 22.
He was pointing to a prophecy unfolding before their eyes.
This is where the story becomes impossible to ignore.
David wrote Psalm 22 approximately one thousand years before Christ.
Crucifixion as a Roman method of execution did not yet exist.
Yet the details read like eyewitness testimony from Calvary.
Psalm 22:7 says:
"All who see me mock me; they hurl insults, shaking their heads."
Now compare the crucifixion:
"Those who passed by hurled insults at Him, shaking their heads."
(Matthew 27:39)
The language is nearly identical.
Not similar.
Not vaguely related.
Identical in substance.
The scene continues.
Psalm 22:8:
"He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD rescue him."
At the cross:
"He trusts in God. Let God rescue Him now if He wants Him."
(Matthew 27:43)
Again, the same mockery.
The same challenge.
The same contempt.
The same moment.
A thousand years apart.
Then comes one of the most astonishing passages in all Scripture.
Psalm 22:16.
The Hebrew text preserved through history reads:
"כָּאֲרִי יָדַי וְרַגְלָי"
kā'ari yadai v'raglai

A textual issue exists here that scholars have carefully examined. Some ancient manuscript traditions and early witnesses, including the Greek Septuagint, support a reading that carries the sense of "they pierced my hands and my feet."
The Septuagint, translated centuries before Jesus, renders the phrase:
"ὤρυξαν χεῖράς μου καὶ πόδας"
"They pierced my hands and my feet."
This understanding became widely accepted among early Jewish and Christian interpreters because it fits both the surrounding context and the progression of the psalm.
Whatever side one takes regarding the textual discussion, the imagery remains remarkable.
The sufferer is surrounded.
His body is under attack.
His hands and feet become central to the suffering.
Then David writes:
(Psalm 22:17)
Victims of crucifixion often hung in ways that stretched the body and made bones visibly prominent beneath the skin.
The description is striking.
Then comes another detail that feels almost impossible.
Psalm 22:18:
"They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing."
In Hebrew:
"יְחַלְּקוּ בְגָדַי לָהֶם וְעַל־לְבוּשִׁי יַפִּילוּ גוֹרָל"
Yechallequ begadai lahem, ve'al levushi yappilu goral.
"They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing."
Now listen to John's account:
"When the soldiers crucified Jesus, they took His clothes... Let us not tear it. Let's cast lots for it."
John specifically says this happened to fulfill Scripture.
Not because someone manipulated events.
Not because Jesus arranged it.
Roman soldiers were gambling.
Completely unaware they were participating in a prophecy written centuries earlier.
This is where skeptics often pause.
Because many details could theoretically be staged.
But soldiers dividing garments?
Casting lots?
Mockers repeating specific phrases?
These were actions of Christ's enemies.
Not His followers.
Not His supporters.
Not people trying to prove prophecy.
His enemies unknowingly became participants in God's redemptive script.
Yet Psalm 22 does something even more extraordinary.
The psalm refuses to end in despair.
The suffering servant is not abandoned forever.
The agony gives way to victory.
The lament becomes triumph.
The darkness becomes hope.
David suddenly shifts from suffering to worldwide worship.
"All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD."
(Psalm 22:27)
Think about that.
A dying sufferer somehow becomes the reason nations return to God.
A broken body somehow becomes the source of global redemption.
A moment of apparent defeat somehow changes history forever.
That is exactly what happened through Jesus Christ.
The cross looked like scandal.
He was publicly humiliated.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Abandoned by friends.
Condemned as a criminal.
To many watching, this appeared to be the collapse of His mission.
But Heaven saw something different.
What looked like disgrace became salvation.
What looked like failure became victory.
What looked like death became life.
This is the pattern of the Gospel.
And it is the pattern God still uses today.
Because Psalm 22 is not merely about proving prophecy.
It is about revealing the heart of God.
A God who enters suffering.
A God who understands abandonment.
A God who steps into human pain.
A God who rewrites endings.
Some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to stand inside a Psalm 22 season.
The prayers feel unanswered.
The future feels uncertain.
The wounds feel fresh.
You wonder if God sees.
You wonder if God hears.
You wonder if He has forgotten.
But Psalm 22 reminds us that the place where God appears most absent may actually be the place where He is accomplishing His greatest work.
At Calvary, everything looked lost.
Yet redemption was unfolding.
At the cross, evil appeared victorious.
Yet evil was being defeated.
At the tomb, death seemed final.
Yet resurrection was already approaching.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Not because humanity climbed upward toward God.
But because God came downward toward humanity.
Jesus entered our scandal.
Our shame.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our brokenness.
And through His death and resurrection, He offered grace greater than every failure.
The cross is not merely a historical event.
It is God's declaration that no life is beyond redemption.
No failure is beyond forgiveness.
No sinner is beyond grace.
No story is beyond rewriting.
Perhaps that is why Psalm 22 still grips hearts thousands of years later.
Because hidden inside an ancient song of suffering is a promise.
The promise that pain does not get the final word.
The promise that darkness does not get the final word.
The promise that sin does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And because Jesus does, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe today you recognize pieces of yourself in that ancient cry:
"My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?"
If so, keep reading.
Keep believing.
Keep looking toward the cross.
Because the same Psalm that begins with abandonment ends with worship.
The same story that begins in suffering ends in victory.
The same Savior who carried the cross walked out of the tomb.
And the same Christ is still rewriting lives today.
Sit with it.
Pray through it.
What part of Psalm 22 impacted you the most?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
The cross was never the end of the story—it was the pen in the hand of God rewriting it.
